Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

Every category has a bidirectional nature. For example:

One person's sensitivity to the Care/Harm foundation may lead them to support high levels of immigration from poorer nations, to reduce the suffering of those who migrate. Whereas another person's sensitivity to the very same foundation may lead them to oppose those levels, because they believe it could lead to people they care about being harmed.

# Summary of the 1997 Conservative Party Manifesto

## Overview
The 1997 Conservative Party Manifesto, titled "You Can Only Be Sure with the Conservatives," presented a vision for Britain under continued Conservative leadership following 18 years in power. The document emphasized maintaining economic success, promoting individual ownership, and resisting European federalism.

## Economic Achievements and Goals
The manifesto highlighted Britain's economic transformation since 1979, including record low unemployment, inflation below 4% for over four years, and the lowest mortgage rates in 30 years. The Conservatives pledged to maintain tight public spending controls, aiming to reduce the basic income tax rate to 20p and keep Britain as Europe's lowest-tax major economy.

## Employment and Enterprise
Central to the manifesto was job creation through enterprise rather than government intervention. The document strongly opposed the European Social Chapter and national minimum wage, arguing these would destroy jobs by burdening businesses. The party promoted small business growth through reduced corporation tax, simplified regulations, and reformed business rates.

## Families and Ownership
The Conservatives proposed expanding a "property-owning democracy" through continued home ownership programs, employee share schemes, and pension reforms. A revolutionary proposal would provide all young workers with personal pension funds through national insurance rebates. Tax reforms would allow one-earner families to transfer unused personal allowances to working spouses.

## Education
The manifesto promised an "Education Guarantee" with national performance targets, published school results, and intervention in failing schools. It promoted school diversity through grammar schools, specialist schools, and expanded grant-maintained schools while maintaining nursery vouchers for all four-year-olds.

## Healthcare
The NHS received strong commitments for continued real-terms funding increases. Reforms focused on expanding GP services, reducing waiting times, and encouraging private sector investment through the Private Finance Initiative while maintaining free healthcare based on clinical need.

## Law and Order
The Conservatives took credit for four consecutive years of falling crime and promised continued investment in policing, CCTV expansion, and tough sentencing. Mandatory minimum sentences were proposed for persistent burglars and drug dealers. Juvenile crime would be tackled through faster court procedures and parental responsibility orders.

## Europe and Constitution
The manifesto firmly opposed a federal Europe, promising to retain Britain's veto and Social Chapter opt-out. On the single currency, it maintained a "wait and see" position with a referendum guarantee. The party strongly opposed devolution to Scotland and Wales, warning it would threaten the Union.

## Defence and Foreign Policy
Britain's global role was emphasized through NATO membership, UN Security Council participation, and Commonwealth ties. The manifesto committed to maintaining professional armed forces and the nuclear deterrent while adapting to post-Cold War realities.

## Conclusion
The document presented a choice between continued Conservative success and what it characterized as risky Labour alternatives, concluding with 25 specific pledges covering taxation, public services, law and order, and national sovereignty.

# Summary: Labour Party Manifesto 1997 - "New Labour Because Britain Deserves Better"

## Core Vision and Philosophy

The 1997 Labour Manifesto, introduced by Tony Blair, presented "New Labour" as a transformed political party offering a "fresh start" for Britain. The central premise was that Britain could and must do better after 18 years of Conservative rule. The manifesto rejected both old left-wing ideology and Conservative right-wing approaches, positioning New Labour as a modern, pragmatic alternative focused on practical results rather than dogma.

## Ten Key Commitments

The manifesto outlined ten specific pledges forming a "contract with the people":

1. Making education the number one priority with increased spending
2. No increases to basic or top income tax rates
3. Stable economic growth with low inflation
4. Getting 250,000 young unemployed into work
5. Rebuilding the NHS with reduced bureaucracy
6. Being tough on crime and its causes
7. Strengthening families and modernizing welfare
8. Protecting the environment with integrated transport policy
9. Cleaning up politics and decentralizing power
10. Providing leadership in Europe

## Economic Policy

Labour promised fiscal responsibility through a "save to invest" approach rather than "tax and spend." Key commitments included maintaining the 2.5% inflation target, reforming the Bank of England for more effective monetary policy, and sticking to existing public spending limits for the first two years. The windfall levy on privatized utilities would fund welfare-to-work programs. The party pledged no increases in basic or top income tax rates, with a long-term goal of introducing a 10p starting rate.

## Education

Education was declared the "number one priority." Specific policies included reducing class sizes to 30 or under for 5-7 year-olds, guaranteeing nursery places for all four-year-olds, modernizing comprehensive schools with ability-based "setting," connecting schools to information technology, creating a University for Industry for lifelong learning, and implementing zero tolerance for underperforming schools.

## Healthcare

Labour pledged to "save the NHS" by ending the Conservative internal market, cutting bureaucracy, and redirecting savings to patient care. The first £100 million saved would treat an extra 100,000 patients. Primary care would take a leading role, with GPs and nurses planning local health services. A new minister for public health would address root causes of illness, tobacco advertising would be banned, and an independent food standards agency would be established.

## Crime and Justice

The manifesto adopted a "tough on crime, tough on the causes of crime" approach. Policies included halving the time for persistent young offenders from arrest to sentencing, introducing parental responsibility orders, decentralizing the Crown Prosecution Service, creating community safety orders, appointing an anti-drugs supremo, and holding a free parliamentary vote on banning handguns.

## Constitutional Reform

Labour proposed significant democratic renewal: ending hereditary peers' voting rights in the House of Lords, creating devolved parliaments for Scotland and Wales (subject to referendums), establishing an elected mayor and strategic authority for London, incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law, and introducing a Freedom of Information Act. A referendum on voting system reform for the House of Commons was also promised.

## Welfare and Employment

The welfare-to-work program aimed to move 250,000 under-25s from benefits into work through four options: private sector employment with employer rebates, voluntary sector work, full-time study, or environmental taskforce work. The manifesto supported a national minimum wage set by an independent low pay commission, and emphasized that "rights and responsibilities must go hand in hand."

## Europe and Foreign Policy

Labour advocated active engagement in Europe while opposing a federal superstate. Three pre-conditions for joining the single currency were established: Cabinet agreement, Parliamentary approval, and a public referendum. The party committed to signing the Social Chapter, pursuing EU reform, and providing international leadership through a strong defense via NATO while pursuing arms control and human rights promotion.

## Conclusion

The manifesto represented a deliberate repositioning of Labour as a modernized, centrist party capable of economic competence while maintaining social justice commitments—a "third way" between traditional socialism and free-market conservatism.
